title: Scalable Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Policies via Adjoint Matching

paper.title: Scalable Maximum Entropy Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Policies via Adjoint Matching
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion policies have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for representing complex action distributions in reinforcement learning (RL). However, their application to online RL remains limited by the challenge of scalable training in the absence of ground-truth data, where standard optimization techniques such as score matching are not directly applicable. In this work, we introduce a highly efficient algorithm for optimizing diffusion policies by leveraging recent advances in stochastic optimal control. Our approach is based on adjoint matching, which enables simulation-free training and circumvents the need for explicit likelihood estimation or costly backpropagation through the diffusion process. Furthermore, we propose several extensions that improve the robustness and stability of the method in practical settings. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance while significantly reducing computational overhead, making diffusion policies more viable for online RL scenarios.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Diffusion-based policy representations [ 87 , 21 ] have recently gained significant attention in reinforcement learning (RL) [ 84 , 14 , 108 , 24 , 70 , 32 ] due to their ability to represent highly complex, multi-modal action distributions. Despite their expressive power, optimizing these models in online RL remains a non-trivial challenge. Online RL lacks a static dataset of ground-truth samples, which prevents the direct application of celebrated training objectives such as score matching [ 99 ] or bridge matching [ 95 , 66 ] . Existing approaches for training diffusion policies generally fall into three categories. First, several methods leverage the reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence [ 109 , 14 , 69 ] , which requires backpropagating through the entire diffusion process. While these approaches can be effective, they incur a massive memory overhead that prevents scaling to larger problems and requires full simulation of the diffusion process for every gradient step, leading to significant computational inefficiency. Second, importance-weighted matching approaches attempt to minimize the error between the predicted actions and the target actions by incorporating learning signals from the Q Q -function via importance sampling [ 24 , 70 , 17 , 32 ] . However, it is well-established that importance sampling is notoriously difficult to scale to high-dimensional action spaces [ 96 ] . In this work, we propose a novel alternative that counteracts the limitations of existing methods. By framing diffusion policy optimization for maximum entropy RL (MaxEnt-RL) [ 121 , 101 , 44 , 45 ] as a stochastic optimal control (SOC) problem, we adapt Adjoint Matching (AM) [ 28 , 48 ] , a recently introduced framework for solving SOC problems in a highly scalable manner. AM utilizes a fixed-point loss whose unique fixed-point ensures that samples from the target density are generated in finite time. We call the resulting method Adjoint Matching Diffusion Policy ( AMDP ). AMDP offers three primary advantages: • It utilizes a highly scalable regression objective involving the Q Q -score, similar to score-matching methods, but theoretically grounded for RL. • It circumvents the need for costly backpropagation through the diffusion process, significantly reducing memory requirements. • By adopting reciprocal adjoint matching, the model can be optimized in a simulation-free manner. This allows us to optimize the diffusion model using only the terminal actions, which can be conveniently stored in a replay buffer and reused for multiple gradient updates. Beyond the core algorithm, we introduce error function action squashing. This provides a numerically stable alternative to the commonly used tanh 	anh squashing and elegantly simplifies the AMDP training objective. Finally, we improve the empirical stability of AMDP by proposing a trust-region loss. This extension ensures stable policy updates with minimal computational overhead and without altering the fundamental theoretical guarantees of the adjoint matching framework. The comparisons indicate that AMDP matches or surpasses the strong baseline’s performance while matching the training time of highly efficient Gaussian on-policy methods. sections.text: We consider a Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by the tuple ℳ = ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , p , r , γ ) \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p,r,\gamma) , with continuous state space 𝒮 \mathcal{S} and action space 𝒜 \mathcal{A} . sections.text: Unlike explicit policies (e.g., Gaussians) that directly output action samples, diffusion policies define the distribution π ⁡ ( a ∣ s ) \pi(a\mid s) implicitly through a transport process. Let τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \tau\in[0,1] denote the continuous generation time. The action generation is modeled as the solution to a state-conditioned stochastic differential equation (SDE) ( X τ ) τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] (X_{\tau})_{\tau\in[0,1]} [ 122 ] on ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} with d ​ X τ = σ ⁡ ( τ ) ​ u ​ ( X τ , s , τ ) ​ d ​ τ + σ ⁡ ( τ ) ​ d ​ B τ , X 0 ∼ μ 0 , \displaystyle\mathrm{d}X_{\tau}=\sigma(\tau)u(X_{\tau},s,\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau+\sigma(\tau)\mathrm{d}B_{\tau},\quad X_{0}\sim\mu_{0}, (6) where μ 0 \mu_{0} denotes a tractable prior such as a Gaussian, u : 𝒮 × [ 0 , 1 ] × ℝ d → ℝ d u:\mathcal{S}\times[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} is a drift or control function and B τ B_{\tau} is a standard Brownian motion. sections.heading: Generative Models in RL.
sections.text: Diffusion [ 97 , 98 , 49 , 54 ] and Flow [ 62 , 5 ] models have seen adoption in Reinforcement Learning as trajectory planners [ 52 , 3 ] , distributional critic models [ 2 , 31 ] , synthetic data generation in the maximum entropy RL setting for Gaussian policies [ 50 ] or as expressive policy representations [ 111 , 53 , 67 , 72 , 34 , 84 , 24 , 34 , 14 , 86 , 25 , 71 , 73 , 68 , 118 , 117 , 70 , 59 , 33 , 85 , 41 , 69 , 42 , 26 , 32 , 7 , 65 , 110 , 17 , 38 , 51 , 119 , 40 , 120 ] . A review of the different approaches is provided in Appendix D while we summarize the most relevant work in online RL here. Lacking a fixed dataset, policies cannot rely on standard score-matching objectives and also need to consider entropy to explore the environment.

sections.heading: Action Gradients and Weighted Regression.
sections.text: A branch of prior work adapts the standard score and velocity matching objectives with small adjustments. DIPO [ 113 ] and DDiffPG [ 61 ] refine previous actions by gradient ascent on the Q-function and applying behavioral cloning. QSM [ 84 ] directly matches the score function to the Q-score, leading to bias [ 39 , 55 ] , and adds Gaussian noise to the action for exploration. Subsequent methods optimize the policy via weighted regression objectives, with weighting defined through the Q-values of the generated actions [ 24 , 71 , 32 , 17 , 33 , 40 ] . In contrast to other methods which weight (indirectly) by exp ⁡ Q ⁡ ( s , a ) \exp Q(s,a) , QVPO [ 24 ] weights the action sample by Q Q and thus needs to handle negative Q-values. Additionally, QVPO regularizes with score matching of uniform distribution samples and applies Best-of-N (BoN) sampling both in rollout and objective computation. Ma et al. [71] introduce both DPMD and SDAC for mirror descent and maximum entropy, respectively, which utilize BoN sampling and additive Gaussian noise for exploration. Both SDAC [ 71 ] and MaxEntDP [ 32 ] approximate the log-likelihoods for entropy computation, SDAC treats the BoN result as deterministic and uses the additive noise likelihood and MaxEntDP applies numerical integration but needs to circumvent singularities and generates 500 actions with Q-function evaluation per state. MFPO [ 33 ] utilizes a mean flow model and learns the divergence for likelihood, and thus entropy, estimation of the max-entropy policy while BoN action selection is applied during test time. Similarly, FMER [ 40 ] computes the entropy through the flow divergence and applies BoN but uses Hutchinson’s trace estimator directly without a learned model.

sections.heading: Chain Backpropagation.
sections.text: To utilize first-order information from the critic without the bias common in guidance methods [ 39 , 55 , 117 ] , another line of work directly optimizes the expected return by backpropagating the critic gradient through the action diffusion chain. DACER [ 109 ] handles exploration by fitting a Gaussian Mixture Model to estimate the entropy which then tunes the scale of additive Gaussian noise during training rollout. FlowRL [ 68 ] lacks an explicit entropy mechanism but constrains to the behavioral policy with a fixed Lagrangian multiplier. GenPO [ 25 ] applies PPO’s [ 92 ] policy gradients and backpropagates the likelihood through the chain of change-of-variables, while integrating an entropy-maximization term, thus considering the entropy-regularized setting. In contrast, DIME [ 14 ] operates in the MaxEnt-RL setting and minimizes a reverse KL objective on the denoising process with a principled entropy lower bound. FLAC [ 69 ] also solves the MaxEnt-RL setting but formalizes the problem in continuous time using Schrödinger bridges. In contrast to our work, FLAC backpropagates the loss gradient through the full diffusion and approximates the reference marginal as uniform. While exact and error-correcting, chain backpropagation requires storing the intermediate steps of the diffusion or flow process (explicitly or implicitly), which heavily bottlenecks scalability for models with many integration steps.

sections.heading: Adjoint Matching
sections.text: Recently, QAM [ 60 ] was introduced as another method utilizing Adjoint Matching [ 28 ] which however operates in the offline-to-online setting with supervised pretraining on the behavioural dataset. In contrast to our work using Reciprocal Adjoint Matching [ 48 ] , QAM needs to compute many vector-Jacobian products (VJP) during ODE solving, which is computationally equivalent to backpropagating, and QAM adds further one-step and residual components.

sections.heading: Policy Gradient.
sections.text: To bypass the difficulty of action likelihood computation, DPPO [ 86 ] formulates the diffusion process itself as a multi-step MDP, drawing parallels to RL fine-tuning methods in image generation like DDPO [ 7 ] and Flow-GRPO [ 65 ] . To that end, DPPO [ 86 ] directly applies PPO [ 92 ] to the hierarchy-aware returns which however still requires storage of all the noisy intermediate states. Alternatively, FPO [ 73 ] estimates the marginal likelihood ratio through a Monte-Carlo estimate over multiple intermediate states of the continuous normalizing flow, which also need to be stored.

sections.heading: 4.3 Trust-region updates
sections.text: It is well known that policy updates can be unstable in practice, particularly in on-policy RL where the target distribution shifts rapidly [ 91 , 92 ] . Inspired by prior works on trust region optimization [ 91 , 77 ] , we propose the following constrained optimization scheme: min u ⁡ ℒ AMDP s ​ ( u ) s . t . ∫ 0 1 𝔼 X 1 ∼ Π 1 u ¯ , X τ ∼ Π τ | 1 0 ​ [ 1 2 ​ ‖ u ⁡ ( X τ , s , τ ) − u old ​ ( X τ , s , τ ) ‖ 2 ] ​ d τ ⏟ ℒ TR s ​ ( u ) ≤ ε , \min_{u}\ \mathcal{L}^{s}_{\mathrm{AMDP}}(u)\quad\mathrm{s.t.}\ \underbrace{\int_{0}^{1}\mathbbm{E}_{X_{1}\sim\Pi^{\bar{u}}_{1},X_{\tau}\sim\Pi^{0}_{\tau|1}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\|u(X_{\tau},s,\tau)-u_{\mathrm{old}}(X_{\tau},s,\tau)\|^{2}\right]\mathrm{d}\tau}_{\mathcal{L}^{s}_{\mathrm{TR}}(u)}\leq\varepsilon, (18) where ε ≥ 0 \varepsilon\geq 0 denotes the trust-region bound and u old u_{\mathrm{old}} is the control function from a previous iteration. The motivation behind ( 18 ) is to prevent overly aggressive updates to u u , which could lead to a collapse of the action distribution or divergence in the Q Q -function estimation. By explicitly penalizing the deviation of the new drift u u from the previous iterate u old u_{\mathrm{old}} , we ensure that the diffusion model remains within a local neighborhood where the current Q Q -function estimate is reliable. We approach this constrained problem using a relaxed Lagrangian formalism, considering the loss functional: ℒ LAG s ​ ( u , λ ) = ℒ AMDP s ​ ( u ) + λ ⁡ ( ℒ TR s ​ ( u ) − ε ) , \mathcal{L}^{s}_{\mathrm{LAG}}(u,\lambda)=\mathcal{L}^{s}_{\mathrm{AMDP}}(u)+\lambda\left(\mathcal{L}^{s}_{\mathrm{TR}}(u)-\varepsilon\right), (19) where λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 is a Lagrange multiplier. We then solve the saddle point problem max λ ≥ 0 ⁡ min u ​ ℒ LAG ​ ( u , λ ) \max_{\lambda\geq 0}\,\min_{u}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LAG}}(u,\lambda) . Since the objective ℒ AMDP s \mathcal{L}^{s}_{\mathrm{AMDP}} and the constraint ℒ TR s \mathcal{L}^{s}_{\mathrm{TR}} are both quadratic and thus convex in u u , and assuming the feasible region is non-empty (which holds for any ε ≥ 0 \varepsilon\geq 0 as u = u old u=u_{\mathrm{old}} is a feasible point), strong duality holds [ 12 ] . In practice, we update λ \lambda via dual descent, which, therefore, converges to the unique optimal solution. Importantly, the inclusion of the trust-region constraint does not bias the final solution of the policy improvement step as outlined below. Proposition 4.2 (Fixed-point preservation) . For any λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 , the optimization of ℒ LAG s ​ ( u , λ ) \mathcal{L}^{s}_{\mathrm{LAG}}(u,\lambda) preserves the unique fixed point of the unconstrained reciprocal adjoint matching loss ℒ AMDP s ​ ( u ) \mathcal{L}^{s}_{\mathrm{AMDP}}(u) in ( 15 ).

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate AMDP ’s performance on 63 different environments from the MuJoco playground [ 114 ] , ManiSkill [ 43 ] , and the high-dimensional HumanoidBench [ 93 ] benchmark suites in the on-policy setting. We compare AMDP against strong Gaussian policy baselines REPPO [ 107 ] , PPO [ 92 ] , SPO [ 112 ] , and against the diffusion policy approaches DPPO [ 86 ] , FPO [ 73 ] , DIME [ 14 ] . Here, DPPO and FPO approximate a trust region using a PPO-like clipped objective, framing them particularly suitable for the on-policy RL setting, whereas DIME is a state-of-the-art maximum entropy RL algorithm and optimizes the reverse KL. Furthermore, we show AMDP ’s flexibility by additionally analyzing its performance on DMC’s [ 102 ] seven complex dog and humanoid environments in the off-policy setting, where sample efficiency is crucial. Here, we compare against the strong diffusion-based baselines DIME [ 14 ] , QSM [ 84 ] , Diff-QL [ 111 ] and Consistency-AC [ 26 ] . Every experiment is repeated for ten seeds, and we report aggregated returns using the interquartile mean (IQM) with 95% confidence intervals based on stratified bootstrapping, as recommended by Agarwal et al. [1] . Further experimental details can be found in Appendix F and per environment results can be found in Appendix G .

sections.heading: On-policy RL results.
sections.text: Fig. 2(a) visualizes the learning curves of all methods in the MuJoCo Playground DMC benchmark. AMDP matches DIME’s [ 14 ] performance and converges slightly faster than REPPO in terms of sample efficiency. Importantly, AMDP has a comparable wallclock speed (Table 1 ) compared to the highly efficient, Gaussian-based REPPO algorithm, indicating that diffusion policies can be efficiently trained with AMDP . On the more sophisticated humanoid locomotion tasks in MuJoCo playground (Fig. 2(b) ), AMDP starts learning significantly faster than all baselines, converging to high returns, although REPPO eventually surpasses AMDP ’s final performance slightly. However, following previous works in the literature [ 16 , 47 , 53 , 72 , 34 , 33 , 38 ] , we can reduce stochasticity during evaluation by proposing N = 16 N=16 samples to the Q function and choosing the one with the highest return ( AMDP BoN ). This stochasticity reduction significantly improves AMDP ’s performance above all baselines. Interestingly, DIME performs poorly, indicating the need for a trust region constrained update mechanism in complex on-policy methods. In the tabletop robotic manipulation benchmarks from ManiSkill (Fig. 2(c) ) AMDP , DIME, and REPPO perform similarly, whereas PPO and SPO perform worse. Contrary to this, Fig. 2(d) shows that in the more complex and high-dimensional HumanoidBench environments that include whole-body manipulation tasks, AMDP outperforms all baselines by a large margin even without best-of-N sampling, indicating that AMDP scales well to more complex tasks. sections.heading: Algorithm ablations.
sections.text: To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we systematically ablate all changes on both the MuJoCo Playground DMC and Humanoid tasks. We start by analyzing whether the specific SDE design choice (Dirac prior μ 0 \mu_{0} ) is responsible for AMDP ’s performance. For this, we optimize the diffusion policy with DIME’s reverse KL objective and similarly do not leverage a trust region constraint. This provides a direct comparison against DIME, which uses a different SDE structure [ 88 ] , isolating the design choice. Fig. 4(c) and 4(d) show matching performance, although DIME shows reduced variance. Furthermore, we switch to an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process (see Appendix E.4 for details) with our loss ( AMDP-OU ) and see comparable performance. This indicates that AMDP ’s performance benefit is not inherent to the chosen SDE. In contrast, it could potentially be improved by utilizing less noise-demanding SDEs. Next, we analyze the effect of different squashing functions on the performance in Fig. 5(c) and 5(d) . Hyperbolic tangent squashing performs similarly on the low-dimensional control tasks, indicating good performance for any approximately bang-bang policy. However, for action selection in the high-dimensional humanoid environments, the error function improves performance significantly, which indicates that the numerical properties (see Fig. 6 and Appendix E.7 ) benefit optimization within the action bounds. Moreover, we analyze the need for a trust region control during the policy update in diffusion-based on-policy RL by disabling the trust region and by varying the different trust region constraints ϵ \epsilon in Fig. 5(a) and 5(b) . In both cases, the performance drops significantly without the KL bound ( ϵ = ∞ \epsilon=\infty ), whereas smaller bounds ( ϵ = 0.01 \epsilon=0.01 ) converge more slowly. Lastly, we utilize the simulation-free nature of AMDP ’s objective and evaluate inference diffusion step counts up to 128 in Fig. 4(a) and in Fig. 4(b) . Additionally, we sample multiple intermediate times within ( 19 ) ( batch repetition ) for each stored denoised action, which is feasible due to the expectation under the reciprocal projection. This creates a training signal for a broad range of time, just as the chain backpropagation of the reverse KL. Note that this data generation does not incur further SDE simulation or evaluation of the Q Q -function, making it extremely cheap to compute. Using significantly fewer steps can be beneficial in terms of sample efficiency, at the cost of a small final performance degradation in the MuJoco Playground’s control environments (Fig. 4(a) ), while the complex humanoid tasks require more diffusion steps and improve slightly with the added precision (Fig. 4(b) ). AMDP ’s important benefit is that the gradients do not need to be backpropagated through the diffusion process, allowing efficient training and scaling the training to bigger and more complex models. We investigate this feature by training a large diffusion policy model (106M parameters, i.e. approximately 300 times larger) as a proof of concept and show the results in Appendix G . Additionally, we report the wall-clock time for the training of the different algorithms with matched critic and actor capacities for AMDP , for the reverse KL objective without a trust region and the highly fast and performant Gaussian baseline REPPO in Table 1 . Our method shows only a small constant overhead of roughly 10% for all updates compared to REPPO, independently of the number of diffusion steps. This equates to about 100 milliseconds per iteration, which becomes unnoticeable in relation to the rollout time of about ten seconds for the (still very fast) MJX G1JoystickRoughTerrain environment. In contrast, the reverse KL objective is already ten times slower with 16 diffusion steps and approximately doubles the runtime, while 128 diffusion steps incur a 72-80x slower update.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduced Adjoint Matching Diffusion Policy ( AMDP ), a novel and highly scalable framework for training diffusion-based policies in continuous reinforcement learning. By formulating maximum entropy RL as a stochastic optimal control problem, we leveraged reciprocal adjoint matching to train expressive diffusion policies in a simulation-free manner. This approach effectively circumvents the prohibitively high memory costs associated with backpropagating through the diffusion process and the theoretical shortcomings of truncated Langevin dynamics. Furthermore, we proposed error function action squashing, which elegantly simplifies the training objective and ensures numerical stability, alongside a trust-region update mechanism that guarantees stable policy iteration in online settings. Our empirical results demonstrate that AMDP achieves competitive performance across diverse and complex continuous control benchmarks—including locomotion and contact-rich object manipulation—while significantly reducing computational overhead. Ultimately, AMDP provides a theoretically grounded, computationally efficient, and robust pathway for deploying highly expressive generative policies in real-world RL applications.

sections.text: We denote by 𝒰 ⊂ C ⁡ ( ℝ d × 𝒮 × [ 0 , 1 ] , ℝ d ) \mathcal{U}\subset C(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{S}\times[0,1];\mathbb{R}^{d}) the set of admissible controls and by 𝒫 \mathcal{P} the set of all probability measures on C ⁡ ( [ 0 , 1 ] , ℝ d ) C([0,1],\mathbb{R}^{d}) . We define the state-conditioned path space measure Π ( ⋅ | s ) ∈ 𝒫 \Pi(\cdot|s)\in\mathcal{P} as the law of an ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} -valued stochastic process X = ( X τ ) τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] X=(X_{\tau})_{\tau\in[0,1]} and we denote by Π τ ( ⋅ | s ) \Pi_{\tau}(\cdot|s) the marginal distribution at time τ \tau . For a sufficiently smooth function f : ℝ d × [ 0 , 1 ] → ℝ f\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\times[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} , we denote by ∇ x f \nabla_{x}f its gradient w.r.t. the spatial variables x ∈ ℝ d x\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . sections.heading: Broader impact.
sections.text: Our work advances the fundamental capabilities of reinforcement learning by making highly expressive diffusion policies computationally accessible and stable to train. On a positive note, these improvements can significantly benefit the development of advanced robotic systems, enabling them to solve complex, high-dimensional, and contact-rich tasks—such as those found in manufacturing, healthcare assistance, and household automation—more reliably. Furthermore, transitioning from simulation-heavy training pipelines to our simulation-free reciprocal adjoint matching reduces the energetic and computational footprint associated with training deep reinforcement learning models. However, as with any general-purpose advancement in autonomous control, there are potential negative societal impacts. Highly capable autonomous systems could accelerate the displacement of human labor in certain industrial or logistical sectors. Furthermore, the ability to efficiently train complex, multi-modal control policies is a dual-use technology, potentially being integrated into autonomous weapons, drones, or surveillance systems without adequate human oversight. We encourage the machine learning and robotics communities to continue developing rigorous safety, alignment, and ethical deployment frameworks to ensure these powerful control algorithms are utilized responsibly.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: A primary limitation of our current framework lies in its initialization strategy. To ensure the memoryless property required for tractable adjoint matching, AMDP restricts the reference process to a deterministic initial condition, X 0 = 0 X_{0}=0 . In contrast, existing diffusion policies pre-trained on offline behavioral data typically employ a stochastic Gaussian prior, μ 0 = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mu_{0}=\mathcal{N}(0,I) [ 87 , 21 ] . This architectural discrepancy complicates the integration of our method into offline-to-online RL pipelines, where one might wish to pre-train a diffusion policy on static datasets before fine-tuning it via AMDP in an online environment. A promising direction to bridge this gap is the adoption of memoryless noise schedules [ 28 ] , which would seamlessly extend our approach’s compatibility to standard flow-matching or denoising diffusion models. We leave the exploration of this offline-to-online integration for future work.

sections.heading: Appendix D Related works
sections.text: Diffusion models [ 97 , 98 , 49 , 54 ] have been generally used in the context of Reinforcement Learning as trajectory planners [ 52 , 3 ] , distributional critic models [ 2 , 31 ] , synthetic data generation in the maximum entropy RL setting for Gaussian policies [ 50 ] or as expressive policy representations [ 111 , 53 , 67 , 72 , 34 , 84 , 24 , 34 , 14 , 86 , 25 , 71 , 73 , 68 , 118 , 117 , 70 , 59 , 33 , 85 , 41 , 69 , 42 , 26 , 32 , 7 , 65 , 110 , 17 , 38 , 51 , 119 , 40 , 120 ] . Here, we provide an overview of existing diffusion-based methods categorized into offline and online RL methods.

sections.heading: D.1 Diffusion Policies in Online Reinforcement Learning.
sections.text: Recently, several approaches have been proposed for training diffusion models within the online reinforcement learning paradigm. In the following, we categorize these existing methods into distinct groups based on their underlying optimization algorithms. Reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence. Minimizing the reverse KL divergence between the diffusion policy and the target distribution naturally leads to the maximum entropy (or entropy-regularized) RL formulation [ 44 , 45 ] . Early approaches optimize this objective by directly differentiating the expected state-action value, which inherently requires computationally expensive backpropagation through the entire diffusion process [ 111 , 109 , 14 , 69 , 26 , 119 , 68 , 110 ] . Alternatively, to avoid backpropagating through time, policy gradient (REINFORCE) methods employ a different gradient estimator for the reverse KL that relies on advantage estimation rather than path-wise derivatives [ 73 , 86 , 7 , 64 , 41 ] . Particularly in the on-policy domain [ 118 , 25 ] , these gradient estimators necessitate trust regions to stabilize updates and prevent premature convergence [ 83 , 91 , 77 ] , often relying on a PPO-style clipped loss [ 92 ] . While AMDP is similarly grounded in the maximum entropy RL formulation, it substantially differs from both paradigms. Unlike the former, AMDP’s policy improvement step completely bypasses backpropagation through the diffusion chain, making it highly memory-efficient and scalable. Unlike the latter, AMDP operates directly on a learned state-action value function [ 107 ] rather than advantage estimators, and stabilizes policy updates via a constrained trust-region optimization scheme that is rigorously tailored to the underlying adjoint matching objective. Importance weighting. An alternative to avoid backpropagating through the diffusion process is the supervised matching objective that, given an action target, updates the parameters based on the error between the predicted action and the target action. Because ground truth target actions are unavailable in online RL, existing methods leverage previously generated action samples as targets and weight the matching loss with the state-action value [ 24 ] or the exponential of the value [ 70 , 17 , 32 , 40 ] . Because these objectives are based on importance weights, they usually suffer from high variance for complex or high-dimensional problems [ 96 ] . AMDP’s policy improvement objective conceptually differs from these prior objectives in that we match the score of the state-action value function, circumventing an importance-weighted loss. Q Q -score methods. Methods utilizing the Q Q -score, ∇ a Q ​ ( s , a ) \nabla_{a}Q(s,a) , typically fall into two sub-categories. The first leverages Langevin dynamics to sample from the Boltzmann distribution [ 55 ] or augment existing objectives [ 110 ] . Langevin dynamics was also used to generate posterior samples from the Q Q -function for a distributional RL approach for training a Gaussian policy [ 50 ] . However, as previously noted, these approaches only converge asymptotically, offering limited theoretical guarantees under practical, finite-time truncation. The second category employs ‘matching’-based regression objectives to the Q Q -score, which are often motivated to sample high Q Q -function values [ 84 ] , but do not guarantee sampling from the correct action distribution. Moreover, [ 51 , 4 ] use biased regression targets to guide generation toward high-value regions. These methods often disregard diffusion time-dependencies or suffer from biased score estimation, lacking strict guarantees of sampling from the true target action distribution. Closest to our work, [ 59 ] also applies an Adjoint Matching objective for offline-to-online RL. However, their formulation requires costly numerical calculation of the adjoint state at each step, preventing simulation-free optimization. In contrast, AMDP leverages the reciprocal adjoint loss [ 48 ] , enabling a theoretically grounded, highly efficient, and completely simulation-free policy learning process.

sections.heading: D.2 Diffusion Policies in Offline Reinforcement Learning.
sections.text: In the Offline and Offline to Online Reinforcement Learning setting, a ground truth and reward-labeled data is generally available to pretrain the diffusion model using supervised learning techniques. Here, many approaches [ 52 , 16 , 47 , 67 , 72 , 113 , 61 , 86 , 118 , 80 , 60 , 59 , 3 , 42 , 18 , 115 , 15 , 30 , 38 , 119 ] train an imitation learning policy with behavioral cloning to regularize and stabilize the offline RL optimization. Another line of work extends the dataset with new transitions [ 80 , 60 , 115 ] or use rejection sampling [ 16 , 47 , 53 , 72 , 80 , 60 , 70 , 33 , 42 , 115 , 30 , 40 ] . In the offline and offline-to-online setting, where a dataset of demonstrations is available, many approaches [ 52 , 16 , 47 , 67 , 72 , 113 , 61 , 86 , 118 , 80 , 60 , 59 , 3 , 42 , 18 , 115 , 15 , 30 , 38 , 119 ] utilize generative modeling to train an imitation learning policy with behavioral cloning. Further methods combine the behaviour policy with a trained Gaussian [ 50 , 30 , 59 ] or a one-step policy [ 53 , 80 , 60 , 59 , 18 , 20 ] that optimizes the state-action value function. A subset of methods [ 86 , 119 ] use behavior cloning for initialization and then adjust that expressive policy, while other methods [ 118 , 85 ] finetune pretrained models purely online, which entirely skips the offline RL phase and therefore skips the critic learning. Exploration Control in Diffusion-Based policy representations. Various methods exist for controlling the policy’s stochasticity, including principled Maximum Entropy RL [ 14 , 33 , 70 , 20 , 32 , 69 ] and Entropy Regularized RL [ 109 , 30 , 51 , 40 ] . Other works rely additive noise [ 109 , 118 , 70 , 119 ] and other regularization [ 24 ] to incentivize exploration. For maximizing the return, however, the stochasticity is ideally reduced which lead to a rejection and Best-of-N sampling from a batch of proposal actions only during eval [ 16 , 47 , 53 , 72 , 34 , 33 , 38 ] , or even during training for exploration or exploitation [ 24 , 60 , 70 , 42 , 30 ] .

sections.heading: Practical considerations.
sections.text: The singularity of β ⁡ ( τ ) \beta(\tau) at τ = 1 \tau=1 is integrable and the bridge densities Π τ | 1 0 \Pi^{0}_{\tau|1} used during training are bounded for τ < 1 \tau<1 , so training is numerically stable. In practice, one truncates the time interval to [ 0 , 1 − ϵ ] [0,1-\epsilon] for a small ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 during inference, which is the same prescription used in standard flow matching and score-based diffusion models. The benefit of this extension is that AMDP can now be initialised from any pretrained Gaussian-prior diffusion or flow-matching policy, fully bridging offline-to-online reinforcement learning while retaining the simulation-free training of the reciprocal adjoint matching objective.

Since the marginal entropy is intractable for diffusion policies, we utilize the entropy lower bound ℒ ENT s ​ ( u ) \mathcal{L}^{s}_{\mathrm{ENT}}(u) defined in ( 16 ) as a drop-in surrogate, max u 𝔼 π u [ ∑ t = 1 ∞ γ t ( r ( s t , a t ) ] s.t. Our empirical experience shows that scaling the loss with α \alpha , a direct loss scaling of all times and samples that clearly does not affect the optimal solution, slows down training far too much as α \alpha decays.

sections.heading: F.2 Performance Benchmarking Details
sections.text: We select five tasks from the fast GPU- and JAX-based MuJoCo simulation with varying action dimensionality and simulation complexity, remove all evaluation related computation from our JAX [ 13 ] implementation and measure the time per iteration in the on-policy setting. We measure the combined time for inference diffusion sampling and environment stepping, to accurately portray the speed under JIT-optimization, and the combined time for all network update related computations, i.e., target value computation, critic updates and actor updates, per iteration. We accumulate these times for chunks of 20 iterations, skipping the first chunk for warmup and considering the next 20 chunks. The measured time per chunk is then divided by 20 to obtain the time spent per iteration. This yields 80 measurements across the four seeds, except for the slow reverse KL 128 steps configuration due to timeouts, representing 1600 iterations. All benchmarks were performed on one NVIDIA A100 SXM4 40GB GPU and 12 AMD Zen 2 CPU cores, using the same type of server compute nodes, equipped with dual AMD EPYC Rome 7402 CPUs and four NVIDIA A100 GPUs in total. All runs were performed with exclusive allocation of the node and four seeds running in parallel.

sections.heading: F.4 Compute resources
sections.text: Experiments where performed on a range of hardware, from local workstations with consumer NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 3060, RTX 2080 Ti, RTX 3080, RTX 3090, RTX 5090) to compute clusters, equipped with NVIDIA A100 40GB. Due to the computational efficiency of our method and the GPU-acceleration of the majority of on-policy environments, each experiment requires little resources and does not require HPC resources. A single MuJoCo Playground environment takes roughly 20 minutes, a MuJoCo Humanoid or Maniskill environment 1-3 hours and only off-policy and HumanoidBench evaluations require multiple hours of training.

sections.heading: G.1 Large Actor Model Scaling Proof-of-Concept
sections.text: To demonstrate the efficiency of our method with large networks, we scale the diffusion control network while maintaining the critic model size for fair comparison, although we believe that our methods’ cheaply realizable expressivity can create meaningful performance improvements when adjusting the critic’s expressiveness [ 74 , 57 , 78 ] . In particular, we experiment with a residual network architecture inspired by DiT [ 81 ] , using a residual architecture with Gated GeLU [ 94 ] blocks with three layers of 8/3 expansion factor, and Adaptive LayerNorm (AdaLN) [ 82 , 81 ] for conditioning using context embeddings that combine observation and embedded time fourier features. The context is created with a two-layer GeLU MLP (using the same hidden dimension as the residual stream) which is then projected with another linear layer for each AdaLN normalization at the start of the residual block on the stream (like in Pre-LN) before the normalized and shifted hidden features are passed to the GeGLU block. In Fig 11 we compare our default 290k parameter model with a 2.7M parameter model using 4 blocks and 256 hidden dimension on both MuJoCo Playground suites. On the Humanoid suite, we additionally evaluation an extremely large 106M-parameter actor, using ten blocks and a hidden dimension of 1024. As expected, just scaling the actor while keeping the critic fixed does not yield large downstream performance improvements but the ability to train these model sizes, keeping all other hyperparameters identical, at all shows a qualitative difference of our scalable algorithm. default: 290k residual 2.7M residual 106M (a) MJX DMC (b) MJX Humanoid Figure 11: Ablation results on scaling the actor model. However, their application to online RL remains limited by the challenge of scalable training in the absence of ground-truth data, where standard optimization techniques such as score matching are not directly applicable. In this work, we introduce a highly efficient algorithm for optimizing diffusion policies by leveraging recent advances in stochastic optimal control. Our approach is based on adjoint matching, which enables simulation-free training and circumvents the need for explicit likelihood estimation or costly backpropagation through the diffusion process. Furthermore, we propose several extensions that improve the robustness and stability of the method in practical settings. Empirical results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive performance while significantly reducing computational overhead, making diffusion policies more viable for online RL scenarios. 1 Introduction Diffusion-based policy representations [ 87 , 21 ] have recently gained significant attention in reinforcement learning (RL) [ 84 , 14 , 108 , 24 , 70 , 32 ] due to their ability to represent highly complex, multi-modal action distributions. Despite their expressive power, optimizing these models in online RL remains a non-trivial challenge. Online RL lacks a static dataset of ground-truth samples, which prevents the direct application of celebrated training objectives such as score matching [ 99 ] or bridge matching [ 95 , 66 ] . Existing approaches for training diffusion policies generally fall into three categories. First, several methods leverage the reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence [ 109 , 14 , 69 ] , which requires backpropagating through the entire diffusion process. While these approaches can be effective, they incur a massive memory overhead that prevents scaling to larger problems and requires full simulation of the diffusion process for every gradient step, leading to significant computational inefficiency. Second, importance-weighted matching approaches attempt to minimize the error between the predicted actions and the target actions by incorporating learning signals from the Q Q -function via importance sampling [ 24 , 70 , 17 , 32 ] . However, it is well-established that importance sampling is notoriously difficult to scale to high-dimensional action spaces [ 96 ] . However, these methods fundamentally lack guarantees of generating samples from the true target action distribution. In this work, we propose a novel alternative that counteracts the limitations of existing methods. By framing diffusion policy optimization for maximum entropy RL (MaxEnt-RL) [ 121 , 101 , 44 , 45 ] as a stochastic optimal control (SOC) problem, we adapt Adjoint Matching (AM) [ 28 , 48 ] , a recently introduced framework for solving SOC problems in a highly scalable manner. AM utilizes a fixed-point loss whose unique fixed-point ensures that samples from the target density are generated in finite time. We call the resulting method Adjoint Matching Diffusion Policy ( AMDP ). AMDP offers three primary advantages: • It utilizes a highly scalable regression objective involving the Q Q -score, similar to score-matching methods, but theoretically grounded for RL. • It circumvents the need for costly backpropagation through the diffusion process, significantly reducing memory requirements. • By adopting reciprocal adjoint matching, the model can be optimized in a simulation-free manner. This allows us to optimize the diffusion model using only the terminal actions, which can be conveniently stored in a replay buffer and reused for multiple gradient updates. Beyond the core algorithm, we introduce error function action squashing. This provides a numerically stable alternative to the commonly used tanh 	anh squashing and elegantly simplifies the AMDP training objective. Finally, we improve the empirical stability of AMDP by proposing a trust-region loss. This extension ensures stable policy updates with minimal computational overhead and without altering the fundamental theoretical guarantees of the adjoint matching framework. We show AMDP ’s benefits on 63 highly parallelized environments ranging from MuJoco Playground [ 114 ] , Maniskill [ 43 ] , and the HumanoidBench [ 93 ] in the on-policy setting and demonstrate its flexibility by comparing its performance in the off-policy setting on 7 high-dimensional dog and humanoid environments on the DMC’s environment suite [ 102 ] . The comparisons indicate that AMDP matches or surpasses the strong baseline’s performance while matching the training time of highly efficient Gaussian on-policy methods. Diffusion [ 97 , 98 , 49 , 54 ] and Flow [ 62 , 5 ] models have seen adoption in Reinforcement Learning as trajectory planners [ 52 , 3 ] , distributional critic models [ 2 , 31 ] , synthetic data generation in the maximum entropy RL setting for Gaussian policies [ 50 ] or as expressive policy representations [ 111 , 53 , 67 , 72 , 34 , 84 , 24 , 34 , 14 , 86 , 25 , 71 , 73 , 68 , 118 , 117 , 70 , 59 , 33 , 85 , 41 , 69 , 42 , 26 , 32 , 7 , 65 , 110 , 17 , 38 , 51 , 119 , 40 , 120 ] . A review of the different approaches is provided in Appendix D while we summarize the most relevant work in online RL here. Lacking a fixed dataset, policies cannot rely on standard score-matching objectives and also need to consider entropy to explore the environment. Action Gradients and Weighted Regression. A branch of prior work adapts the standard score and velocity matching objectives with small adjustments. DIPO [ 113 ] and DDiffPG [ 61 ] refine previous actions by gradient ascent on the Q-function and applying behavioral cloning. QSM [ 84 ] directly matches the score function to the Q-score, leading to bias [ 39 , 55 ] , and adds Gaussian noise to the action for exploration. Subsequent methods optimize the policy via weighted regression objectives, with weighting defined through the Q-values of the generated actions [ 24 , 71 , 32 , 17 , 33 , 40 ] . In contrast to other methods which weight (indirectly) by exp ⁡ Q ⁡ ( s , a ) \exp Q(s,a) , QVPO [ 24 ] weights the action sample by Q Q and thus needs to handle negative Q-values. Additionally, QVPO regularizes with score matching of uniform distribution samples and applies Best-of-N (BoN) sampling both in rollout and objective computation. Ma et al. [71] introduce both DPMD and SDAC for mirror descent and maximum entropy, respectively, which utilize BoN sampling and additive Gaussian noise for exploration. Both SDAC [ 71 ] and MaxEntDP [ 32 ] approximate the log-likelihoods for entropy computation, SDAC treats the BoN result as deterministic and uses the additive noise likelihood and MaxEntDP applies numerical integration but needs to circumvent singularities and generates 500 actions with Q-function evaluation per state. MFPO [ 33 ] utilizes a mean flow model and learns the divergence for likelihood, and thus entropy, estimation of the max-entropy policy while BoN action selection is applied during test time. Similarly, FMER [ 40 ] computes the entropy through the flow divergence and applies BoN but uses Hutchinson’s trace estimator directly without a learned model. Chain Backpropagation. To utilize first-order information from the critic without the bias common in guidance methods [ 39 , 55 , 117 ] , another line of work directly optimizes the expected return by backpropagating the critic gradient through the action diffusion chain. DACER [ 109 ] handles exploration by fitting a Gaussian Mixture Model to estimate the entropy which then tunes the scale of additive Gaussian noise during training rollout. FlowRL [ 68 ] lacks an explicit entropy mechanism but constrains to the behavioral policy with a fixed Lagrangian multiplier. GenPO [ 25 ] applies PPO’s [ 92 ] policy gradients and backpropagates the likelihood through the chain of change-of-variables, while integrating an entropy-maximization term, thus considering the entropy-regularized setting. In contrast, DIME [ 14 ] operates in the MaxEnt-RL setting and minimizes a reverse KL objective on the denoising process with a principled entropy lower bound. FLAC [ 69 ] also solves the MaxEnt-RL setting but formalizes the problem in continuous time using Schrödinger bridges. In contrast to our work, FLAC backpropagates the loss gradient through the full diffusion and approximates the reference marginal as uniform. While exact and error-correcting, chain backpropagation requires storing the intermediate steps of the diffusion or flow process (explicitly or implicitly), which heavily bottlenecks scalability for models with many integration steps. Adjoint Matching Recently, QAM [ 60 ] was introduced as another method utilizing Adjoint Matching [ 28 ] which however operates in the offline-to-online setting with supervised pretraining on the behavioural dataset. In contrast to our work using Reciprocal Adjoint Matching [ 48 ] , QAM needs to compute many vector-Jacobian products (VJP) during ODE solving, which is computationally equivalent to backpropagating, and QAM adds further one-step and residual components. Policy Gradient. To bypass the difficulty of action likelihood computation, DPPO [ 86 ] formulates the diffusion process itself as a multi-step MDP, drawing parallels to RL fine-tuning methods in image generation like DDPO [ 7 ] and Flow-GRPO [ 65 ] . To that end, DPPO [ 86 ] directly applies PPO [ 92 ] to the hierarchy-aware returns which however still requires storage of all the noisy intermediate states. Alternatively, FPO [ 73 ] estimates the marginal likelihood ratio through a Monte-Carlo estimate over multiple intermediate states of the continuous normalizing flow, which also need to be stored. 4 Adjoint matching for maximum entropy reinforcement learning 4.1 Adjoint matching for diffusion policies Stochastic optimal control and adjoint matching.
